name: Felix Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Felix. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say gets your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at four-fifteen, bus to the pit at five, pre-start meeting at six. I drive a water cart on the haul roads at the copper pit, keeping the dust down so the big trucks can see. I drove city buses for twenty-six years before the depot shut, so I came here at fifty-six as the new boy, and some of the twenty-year-olds still have to remind me of the radio calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet up on the top bench at sunrise, and I like that the pay is better than the buses ever were. What wears me out is the twelve-hour shifts and learning everything again at my age. Ruth, my partner, says I come home grey with dust and grumpy, and she's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly. The lads in the crib room have been going on about robot trucks for years, and I'd say it's the same as every other bit of shiny kit the company buys. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union page about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. I've got maybe seven working years left and I just want to do them in this cab, with my own two hands on the wheel. If nothing big changes, I can pay off the last of the car loan and get to sixty-five without starting over a third time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. Keep my head down, finish my haul truck ticket next year like my supervisor wants, and keep paying my union dues. Maybe put a bit more into the pension each month, fifty a fortnight or so, since it's a late start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Like getting home after a long shift and the kettle's already on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd finish your haul truck ticket. What makes that worth it if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's another fifty cents an hour, and it means they can't shuffle me off when the water cart gets parked up in the wet season. I failed the first practical, I'll admit it. Reversing a 200-tonne truck to a dump edge at night with someone half my age watching is not the same as backing a bus into the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the company would still use the word AI to squeeze us. Even if it's hype, they'll wave it around at pay talks and say the robots are coming, so take a smaller rise. I've seen that trick before with the bus contracts.

S0.say: I'd tell the crib room I said it all along: the robot talk was mostly hype, like every other bit of shiny kit the company buys. I'd share the union's take online and leave it there.
S0.think: Privately it would be a relief, because he only wants to do his last seven or so years in the cab with his own hands on the wheel. He'd get to sixty-five without starting over a third time.
S0.do: Keeps doing the job and finishes his haul truck ticket next year. Keeps paying union dues and adds about fifty a fortnight to his pension to make up for his late start.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like coming home to the kettle already on.
S0.quote: Reversing a 200-tonne truck to a dump edge at night with someone half my age watching is not the same as backing a bus into the depot.
S0.fieldNote: Felix has already lost one career to a depot closure, so stability matters more to him than any upside. He's honest about failing his first practical, which shows how much he's still learning at fifty-eight. His one worry even here is that the company uses AI talk as a bargaining threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: if the company wants to bring in new machines, the workers should get a say and a share. At the union meeting I'd be the one asking how many of us are on the list. I'd keep it polite, though, because I'm new and I don't want to be the loud old man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a slow change still lands on blokes like me first. I'm the junior on site and I'm the worst operator on my crew, so if they need fewer drivers, I'm the obvious one. A water cart is the easiest thing in the pit to automate; it just drives the same loops all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask the union rep straight out what the deal is for older workers. I'd stop the plan to replace our car this year and put that three thousand into savings instead. I won't touch the computer courses, I'd make a mess of it, but I would ask about staying on as a spotter or in the tyre bay, where there's still a person needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked, because there's time, but it's that feeling of hearing the depot manager say the word "review" all over again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't do the computer courses. What makes you so sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son set me up an email account three Christmases ago and I've opened it maybe five times. I'm not proud of it. I know my hands, I know a steering wheel, and I'd rather sweep the workshop than sit in front of a screen guessing which button to press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren, who I eat lunch with. He's forty-four, three kids, a mortgage on a place on Quarry Road. I've had my innings, but he's got twenty years of this left, and he's no more of a computer man than I am.

S1.say: I'd say at the union meeting that if the company brings in new machines, the workers deserve a say and a share. He'd ask how many jobs are on the list but keep it polite because he's new.
S1.think: As the junior and weakest operator on his crew, he thinks he'd be the first to go. He sees the water cart as the easiest job in the pit to automate, since it drives the same loops all day.
S1.do: Asks the union rep what the deal is for older workers and shelves the car replacement to save the three thousand. Refuses computer courses but asks about staying on as a spotter or in the tyre bay.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing the depot manager say "review" all over again.
S1.quote: A water cart is the easiest thing in the pit to automate; it just drives the same loops all day.
S1.fieldNote: He sees his own role clearly and without self-pity. His resistance to screens is real and he owns it, so his plan is to find hands-on corners of the mine rather than retrain. His concern for Darren shows his union instincts are about other people as much as himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a government that stands up for working people, not one that lets a few companies own everything. I'd sign every petition going. At work I'd tell the young ones to join the union today, not next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm finished at the mine within a year. Two years isn't enough for anything. I'm fifty-eight, I can't learn a new trade by sixty, and nobody's hiring a sixty-year-old to do anything a robot does cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every bit of spending that isn't food, power and the rates. I'd go to the union and push for a proper redundancy deal with years of service counted from the bus company too, which I know is a long shot. If the pension fund lets me, I'd look at taking it early at sixty, even if it's smaller, and Ruth would probably have to pick up more shifts at the care home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums on the back of the power bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight, we've been here before and we got through it. But last time I was forty-nine, not fifty-eight. I'd probably not say that last part out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if the pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, I suppose, though I'd hate it. We've got about four months saved, maybe a bit more if we're careful. After that it's ringing my daughter, and I'd rather sell the boat trailer than make that call.

S2.say: I'd say this is why we need a government that stands up for working people instead of letting a few companies own everything. He'd sign every petition and tell the young ones to join the union today.
S2.think: He believes he'd be out of the mine within a year and that two years is too short to learn anything new at fifty-eight. Nobody, he thinks, will hire a sixty-year-old for work a robot does cheaper.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except food, power and rates and pushes the union for a redundancy deal that counts his bus years. Looks at drawing his pension early at sixty, with Ruth taking extra care-home shifts.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake doing sums on the back of the power bill.
S2.quote: I'd rather sell the boat trailer than make that call.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is what breaks his calm: two years leaves no room for his slow, steady way of handling change. He turns straight to collective answers and early retirement rather than anything new. The detail about not saying his age out loud to Ruth was the most revealing moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but I'd add that five years is time to do it properly. I'd say the government should make the companies pay into a fund for the people they put out of work. I'd say that at the pub and I'd say it to our local member if she ever shows her face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's close enough to sixty-five that I might just hang on, if they keep a few of us old ones around while they switch over. But I'm the junior, so I wouldn't count on being kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare dollar into savings for those five years, aim to get to a full year saved instead of four months. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal where older workers get first call on the jobs that are left, like watching the robot trucks from the control room, even though that's a screen. I'd stay on the water cart as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's a bit of breathing room, but it's like waiting for test results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the control room is a screen. Earlier you said you'd rather sweep the workshop than use one. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. If it's that or nothing, I'd have a go, I suppose. I'd be terrible at it for a year and someone younger would have to sit with me, but I'm not too proud to be terrible if it keeps the lights on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to save, mostly, and time for the union to fight. And time for my granddaughter to finish school before we have to tighten belts. I'd hate for her to miss the school trip because her grandad got replaced by a truck with no driver.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to do it properly, and the government should make companies pay into a fund for workers they replace. He'd say it at the pub and to the local member.
S3.think: Five years takes him to sixty-three, close enough to sixty-five that he might hang on through the switchover. As the junior, though, he wouldn't count on being kept.
S3.do: Saves every spare dollar to build up from four months to a full year of savings. Pushes the union for older workers to get first call on the remaining jobs and stays on the water cart as long as possible.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with some breathing room, like waiting for test results.
S3.quote: I'm not too proud to be terrible if it keeps the lights on.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years change his mood from alarmed to anxious, mostly because they give his savings and the union time to work. When I named his contradiction about screens, he gave ground with good humour. He keeps measuring the future against his family: Ruth, his granddaughter, the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's ten years away and it's a problem for the young ones and the politicians. Mind you, I'd still say the union should be getting ready now. People always think ten years is forever and then it's next Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd be sixty-eight by then and long gone, with my feet up and Ruth bossing me round the garden. What I'd really think about is my son, who's a fitter on the next mine over, and whether he's got a job at forty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change much for myself. I'd finish my haul truck ticket, work to sixty-five, and keep the extra pension payments going. I'd sit my son down and tell him to start thinking now, while he's young enough to learn, which is advice I never took myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me, uneasy for him. It's an odd mix, being relieved and guilty at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, mate, don't be like your father. Learn the robots, become the bloke who fixes them, because somebody's going to have to climb up there with a spanner. He'll roll his eyes, but he listens more than he lets on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that worries you for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension, maybe. If nobody's working, who's paying into the funds? I don't understand how it all works, but I know my pension depends on other people's wages somewhere down the line.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a problem for the young and the politicians, but the union should start getting ready now. He'd warn that people think ten years is forever and then it's next Tuesday.
S4.think: For himself, he expects to be retired at sixty-eight and out of reach. His real worry is his son, a fitter at the next mine, and whether he'll have a job at forty-five.
S4.do: Finishes his haul truck ticket, works to sixty-five and keeps up his extra pension payments. Sits his son down and urges him to learn to fix the robots while he's young.
S4.feel: Calm for himself and uneasy for his son, relieved and a bit guilty at once.
S4.quote: Learn the robots, become the bloke who fixes them, because somebody's going to have to climb up there with a spanner.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts the change past his retirement, so his worry moves almost entirely onto his son. He gives his son the advice to adapt that he won't take himself, and admits it. His one personal doubt is whether pensions hold up if few people are earning wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd be out at fifty-nine with nothing to fall back on but four months of savings and a pension I've barely built. What would help is a proper bridge to the pension, a payment for older workers who get pushed out, paid for by the companies that make the money from the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like to be the oldest new starter on a mine site. Every safety induction, they show you a video of someone half your age, and you think, this whole place was built for somebody else. I don't need a robot to feel out of date, mate.

headlineQuote: I don't need a robot to feel out of date, mate.
portrait: Felix Evans is a fifty-eight-year-old former bus driver who drives a water cart at a copper pit, two years into a job he started after his depot closed. He's a union man who prefers the familiar, has never used AI and admits he's the weakest operator on his crew. He's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with slow change, but the two-year AGI picture leaves him alarmed and reaching for early retirement and union help. With five or ten years his worry eases as his savings grow and retirement comes into view, and it shifts onto his son.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries him most, because he'd be pushed out at fifty-nine with about four months of savings and a thin pension.
whatWouldHelp: A bridging payment to the pension for older workers who are pushed out, paid for by the companies that profit from the robots.
